Keysight Unites RF and Photonic Design for Tower Semiconductorby Daniel Nenni on 11-25-2026 at 8:00 am

View Profile

View Articles

Private Message

Categories: EDA, Keysight EDA

Key takeaways ▼
Advanced Design System (ADS) Photonic Designer
Keysight Technologies has certified its Advanced Design System (ADS) Photonic Designer for Tower Semiconductor’s PH18 silicon photonics process design kits, bringing electronic and photonic circuit development into a shared environment. Announced November 9, the integration lets engineers move from schematics through simulation and layout while evaluating how electronic circuits and photonic integrated circuits work together. The Tower PH18 kit is available now.
The immediate significance is practical: designers using ADS for radio frequency and high-speed electronics can add Tower photonics to an established workflow. Tower’s RF technologies have been supported in ADS for more than a decade. Extending that relationship to photonics gives engineering teams a more direct way to investigate complete systems before committing a design to fabrication.
Optical communications still depend on electronics at both ends. A transmitter converts electrical information into light, and a receiver converts it back. Between those endpoints, drivers, modulators, optical channels, detectors and amplifiers influence the final signal. Evaluating individual components separately can obscure interactions that determine whether the complete connection meets its performance target.
Keysight’s broader electrical-optical-electrical simulation approach addresses that problem by modeling the signal chain within ADS. Its application materials describe analysis of multiwavelength links, electrical and optical impairments, and receiver signal quality. Engineers can examine how a change in one domain affects another, rather than treating optical transmission as an isolated subsystem.
That capability becomes more consequential as data center interconnects advance toward 1.6 terabits per second and beyond. Faster links leave less room for signal degradation, while AI infrastructure increases pressure to deliver bandwidth efficiently. The engineering question extends beyond whether a photonic device performs well: teams need to understand how it behaves alongside the electronics driving and receiving its signals.
The PH18 integration connects those investigations to a specific manufacturing platform. Tower’s kit supplies component models grounded in device physics, allowing designers to assess photonic behavior within a larger electronic and optical system. ADS also supports photonic layout elements that meet design rules and designer-level comparisons between layouts and schematics. Final foundry verification and tapeout remain in Tower’s tools.
Why does this matter commercially?
The clearest potential benefit is earlier discovery of expensive mistakes. If engineers identify an unsuitable interface or performance bottleneck during simulation, they can revise the design before manufacturing. That could reduce repeated fabrication cycles and shorten development schedules, although the announcement provides no quantified customer results or independent benchmarks establishing those savings.
There is also a collaboration benefit. Electronic and photonic specialists often approach a system through different models, assumptions and tools. A shared simulation environment can give them a common basis for discussing tradeoffs. In practice, that could make it easier to decide whether an observed limitation belongs in the driver, optical circuit or receiver, and where a redesign would have the greatest effect.
The announcement also supports the industry’s interest in co-packaged optics and near-package optics, which bring optical connectivity closer to computing or switching electronics. Keysight’s Photonic Designer materials identify both as applications for its integrated workflow. As physical integration increases, evaluating the electrical and optical portions together becomes a more useful basis for architectural decisions.
For Tower, the strategic opportunity is to make its photonics process easier for existing ADS users to evaluate and adopt. For Keysight, foundry-specific support strengthens the connection between system simulation and implementable circuit design. These are reasonable implications of the integration, rather than evidence that either company has already secured additional customers or revenue.
Bottom line: The development’s importance therefore lies in reducing the distance between an attractive optical concept and a design ready for manufacturing. Better coordination between electronics, photonics and foundry models can help teams make more informed decisions earlier. Success will ultimately depend on model accuracy, usable workflows and agreement between simulated behavior and fabricated hardware. Those measures will determine whether this integration delivers lasting engineering value. For customers, the relevant test is whether those capabilities translate into predictable designs and fewer surprises.
